name: SecurityContext, QoS & downward API
objective: CKAD › Application Design and Build + Observability. Drill EVERY pod-design corner harder than the exam: classic vs native sidecars, init ordering, all three probe types and handlers, lifecycle hooks + graceful shutdown, full securityContext hardening, QoS classes, the Downward API, and a no-hint diagnose-and-fix. Graded exactly, per requirement.

questions.title: Full securityContext hardening (pod + container)
questions.teach:
`securityContext` lives at **pod** and **container** level, and placement matters: `fsGroup` is **pod-only**, while `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `capabilities`, and `allowPrivilegeEscalation` are **container-only**. `runAsNonRoot`/`runAsUser` work at either.

**Gotcha:** `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` needs a writable mount (e.g. an `emptyDir` at `/tmp`) or the app may crash.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `secure-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, running `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) with:
- **Pod-level**: `fsGroup: 2000`, `runAsNonRoot: true`.
- **Container-level**: `runAsUser: 1000`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, capabilities `drop: [ALL]` and `add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]`.
- An `emptyDir` mounted at `/tmp` (so the read-only-root container has a writable path).
questions.hint: `fsGroup` + `runAsNonRoot` go under `spec.securityContext` (pod). `runAsUser`, `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation`, `capabilities` go under the container's `securityContext`. Add an emptyDir volume mounted at /tmp.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: secure-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  securityContext:
    fsGroup: 2000
    runAsNonRoot: true
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    securityContext:
      runAsUser: 1000
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp } ]
  volumes: [ { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} } ]
YAML

verification.description: container: readOnlyRootFilesystem, allowPrivilegeEscalation false, drop ALL + add NET_BIND_SERVICE, emptyDir at /tmp

questions.eli5:
A **securityContext** is the set of safety rules for who your container runs as and what it's allowed to do — like the badge, keycard, and house rules for a worker in a secure building. By default containers often run as root with the keys to everything; hardening dials that way down so a break-in does as little damage as possible.

There are two places to put these rules, and it matters which goes where:

- **Pod level** (applies to everyone in the apartment): `fsGroup: 2000` means "any shared storage is owned by group 2000 so the containers can access it," and `runAsNonRoot: true` is a flat rule "nobody here may be root."
- **Container level** (just this one worker): `runAsUser: 1000` sets the exact employee ID; `readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` glues the whole house shut so nothing can be written; `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false` forbids sneaking extra powers; and `capabilities` trims the keyring — `drop: [ALL]` throws away every special key, then `add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]` hands back just the one that lets you use low-numbered ports.

Because we glued the filesystem shut, we hand the worker one scratch drawer they *can* write to — an emptyDir mounted at `/tmp`.

**Watch out for:**

- **`fsGroup` is pod-only; `readOnlyRootFilesystem`, `capabilities`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation` are container-only.** Put them at the wrong level and it's rejected or ignored. `runAsUser`/`runAsNonRoot` work at either.
- **`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` with no writable mount can crash the app** — give it an emptyDir (here `/tmp`) for anything it needs to write.
- **`runAsNonRoot: true` + `runAsUser: 0` conflict** — the pod fails to start if told to be non-root but assigned UID 0.
- **`drop: [ALL]` then `add:` the few you need** is the right order — drop everything, re-grant selectively.
- **Container-level settings override pod-level** when both set the same thing (e.g. `runAsUser`).
questions.deepDive:
## SecurityContext hardening (pod + container)

### Mental model
`securityContext` controls **who** the process runs as and **what** it may do. It exists at **two levels** — pod (`spec.securityContext`) and container (`spec.containers[].securityContext`) — and **placement matters**: some fields are pod-only, some container-only, a few work at either. Container-level values **override** pod-level for overlapping fields.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  securityContext:                 # POD level
    fsGroup: 2000                  # group that owns mounted volumes
    runAsNonRoot: true             # refuse to run as UID 0
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    securityContext:               # CONTAINER level
      runAsUser: 1000
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
    volumeMounts: [ { name: tmp, mountPath: /tmp } ]   # writable path for RO root
  volumes: [ { name: tmp, emptyDir: {} } ]
```

### Where each field is valid
| Field | Pod | Container | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| `runAsUser` / `runAsGroup` | ✅ | ✅ | UID/GID of the process |
| `runAsNonRoot` | ✅ | ✅ | reject UID 0 at start |
| `fsGroup` | ✅ | ❌ | group owner of mounted volumes |
| `fsGroupChangePolicy` | ✅ | ❌ | when to chown volumes |
| `supplementalGroups` | ✅ | ❌ | extra GIDs |
| `seccompProfile` | ✅ | ✅ | syscall filter |
| `readOnlyRootFilesystem` | ❌ | ✅ | immutable `/` |
| `allowPrivilegeEscalation` | ❌ | ✅ | block gaining new privs |
| `capabilities` | ❌ | ✅ | add/drop Linux capabilities |
| `privileged` | ❌ | ✅ | full host access (avoid) |

### Linux capabilities
- `drop: ["ALL"]` removes every capability, then `add` re-grants only what's needed — least privilege.
- `NET_BIND_SERVICE` lets a non-root process bind ports **<1024** (e.g. 80/443).
- Capability names in the spec **omit the `CAP_` prefix** (`NET_BIND_SERVICE`, not `CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE`).

### readOnlyRootFilesystem
- Makes `/` immutable; the app can only write to explicitly mounted **writable** volumes.
- Give it scratch space (e.g. `emptyDir` at `/tmp`, `/var/run`, `/var/cache`) or writes fail / the app crashes.

### fsGroup
- All files in mounted volumes are owned by GID `fsGroup`, and the volume is made group-writable, so a non-root container can read/write them.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod secure-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.securityContext}'; echo
kubectl -n pod-design get pod secure-pod -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].securityContext}'; echo
kubectl -n pod-design exec secure-pod -- id            # uid=1000 ... gid groups incl 2000
kubectl -n pod-design exec secure-pod -- touch /tmp/x  # OK; touch /x -> read-only FS
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **Level matters:** `fsGroup` pod-only; `readOnlyRootFilesystem`/`capabilities`/`allowPrivilegeEscalation` container-only. Wrong level = schema error or ignored.
- **`readOnlyRootFilesystem: true` without a writable mount** crashes apps that write — add an emptyDir.
- **`runAsNonRoot: true` + `runAsUser: 0`** → pod fails (`container has runAsNonRoot and image will run as root`).
- **Capabilities use no `CAP_` prefix**; drop ALL then add selectively.
- **Container overrides pod** for `runAsUser`/`runAsGroup`/`runAsNonRoot`.
- **`runAsNonRoot` doesn't set a UID** — it only *checks*; pair with `runAsUser` if the image defaults to root.
- Pod Security Admission "restricted" expects `runAsNonRoot`, `allowPrivilegeEscalation: false`, `drop: [ALL]`, and a seccomp profile.

### Quick reference
```yaml
securityContext:                 # pod
  fsGroup: 2000
  runAsNonRoot: true
# container:
  runAsUser: 1000
  readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
  allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
  capabilities: { drop: ["ALL"], add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"] }
```

questions.title: Quality of Service: make a Guaranteed pod
questions.teach:
A pod's **QoS class** is computed from its resources, not set directly. You get **Guaranteed** by making `requests == limits` for **both** cpu and memory on every container. Verify with `kubectl get pod

-o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'`. **Gotcha:** one container missing a limit (or unequal request/limit) drops the whole pod to Burstable.
questions.prompt: Create pod `qos-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`) whose QoS class is **Guaranteed** — set requests and limits **equal**: cpu `200m`, memory `256Mi` for both.
questions.hint: Set `resources.requests` and `resources.limits` to the SAME values (cpu=200m, memory=256Mi). Verify: `kubectl -n pod-design get pod qos-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'` → Guaranteed.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: qos-pod, namespace: pod-design }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
YAML
questions.eli5:
When a node runs low on memory, Kubernetes has to decide who gets kicked out first — like a lifeboat deciding who goes overboard when it's sinking. Your pod's **QoS class** is its priority ticket, and there are three tiers: **Guaranteed** (first-class, evicted last), **Burstable** (middle), and **BestEffort** (steerage, evicted first).

Here's the catch: you don't *pick* your class directly. Kubernetes **calculates** it from how you set your resource **requests** and **limits** (think: "how much I ask for" vs "the ceiling I'm allowed"). To earn the top tier, **Guaranteed**, you must follow one strict rule: for **every** container, set requests **exactly equal to** limits, for **both** CPU and memory. No gaps, no "ask for a little, allow a lot."

So in this task you set cpu `200m` and memory `256Mi` as *both* the request and the limit. Request == limit, for both resources → Kubernetes stamps the pod **Guaranteed**. You can check the stamp with a quick jsonpath query.

**Watch out for:**

- **You can't set QoS directly** — it's computed from resources. Get the resources right and the class follows.
- **Guaranteed is strict:** every container needs requests == limits for BOTH cpu AND memory. One container off, or one resource unequal, drops the whole pod to **Burstable**.
- **Missing a limit entirely** also drops you to Burstable (or BestEffort if nothing is set at all).
- **Units matter:** `200m` = 0.2 CPU; memory `Mi` is mebibytes. Request and limit must match down to the unit.
- **BestEffort** (no requests or limits anywhere) is evicted first under pressure — fine for throwaway work, risky for anything important.
questions.deepDive:
## Quality of Service (QoS) classes

### Mental model
A pod's **QoS class** is **computed by Kubernetes** from its containers' resource `requests`/`limits` — you don't set it directly. It drives **eviction priority** under node resource pressure (and OOM-kill ordering). Three classes: **Guaranteed > Burstable > BestEffort** (BestEffort is evicted first).

### The three classes
| Class | Condition | Evicted |
|---|---|---|
| **Guaranteed** | every container has `requests == limits` for **both** cpu **and** memory | last |
| **Burstable** | at least one request/limit set, but not Guaranteed | middle |
| **BestEffort** | **no** requests or limits on any container | first |

### Guaranteed — the exact rule
For **every** container in the pod:
- `requests.cpu == limits.cpu`, AND
- `requests.memory == limits.memory`.

If any container is missing a limit, or any request ≠ its limit, the pod is **Burstable**.

### The manifest
```yaml
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources:
      requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
      limits:   { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }   # equal → Guaranteed
```

### Resource units
| Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `1` / `1000m` CPU | 1 core |
| `200m` CPU | 0.2 core |
| `256Mi` | 256 mebibytes (2^20 bytes) |
| `256M` | 256 megabytes (10^6 bytes) — **different** from `Mi` |

Request and limit must match **exactly**, same value and unit, to be Guaranteed.

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod qos-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'; echo   # Guaranteed
kubectl -n pod-design describe pod qos-pod | grep -i qos
```

### Why it matters
- **Eviction**: under memory/disk pressure the kubelet evicts BestEffort first, then Burstable using over-request pods, Guaranteed last.
- **OOM score**: Guaranteed containers get the most favourable OOM score; BestEffort the least.
- A Burstable pod exceeding its memory limit is OOM-killed regardless of class.

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **QoS is read-only/computed** — there's no `qosClass` field to set; shape the `resources` instead.
- **Guaranteed needs all four** (cpu+memory, request+limit) **equal on every container** — one gap → Burstable.
- **If only `limits` are set, Kubernetes defaults requests to equal the limits** — that can still yield Guaranteed (cpu+memory), but omit one resource's limit and it drops to Burstable.
- **`Mi` ≠ `M`** — mismatched units make request ≠ limit and break Guaranteed.
- **BestEffort = nothing set anywhere** — risky under pressure.
- Init containers' resources also count toward the class computation.

### Quick reference
```yaml
resources:
  requests: { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
  limits:   { cpu: 200m, memory: 256Mi }
```
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design get pod qos-pod -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'   # Guaranteed
```

questions.title: Downward API: expose pod metadata
questions.teach:
The **Downward API** exposes pod metadata to the app. Use env `valueFrom.fieldRef` for pod fields (`metadata.name`, `metadata.namespace`), env `valueFrom.resourceFieldRef` for a container's `limits`/`requests` (e.g. `limits.cpu`), and a `downwardAPI` **volume** to project fields into files.

**Gotcha:** `metadata.labels`/`annotations` can only be exposed via a **volume**, never an env `fieldRef`.
questions.prompt:
Create pod `downward-pod` in `pod-design` (`busybox:1.36`, container `app`, `sh -c 'sleep 3600'`), labelled `app=downward`, with cpu limit `500m`, exposing:
- env `POD_NAME` ← `metadata.name`, env `POD_NS` ← `metadata.namespace`
- env `CPU_LIMIT` ← `resourceFieldRef` `limits.cpu`
- a `downwardAPI` **volume** mounted at `/podinfo` with an item `labels` ← `metadata.labels`
questions.hint: Env uses `valueFrom.fieldRef` (for metadata.*) and `valueFrom.resourceFieldRef` (for limits.cpu, needs `containerName`). The labels file needs a `downwardAPI` volume with `items: [{path: labels, fieldRef: {fieldPath: metadata.labels}}]`, mounted at /podinfo.
questions.solution:
cat <<'YAML' | kubectl apply -f -
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata: { name: downward-pod, namespace: pod-design, labels: { app: downward } }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources: { limits: { cpu: 500m } }
    env:
    - name: POD_NAME
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
    - name: POD_NS
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.namespace } }
    - name: CPU_LIMIT
      valueFrom: { resourceFieldRef: { containerName: app, resource: limits.cpu } }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: podinfo, mountPath: /podinfo } ]
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items: [ { path: labels, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.labels } } ]
YAML
questions.eli5:
Your app sometimes needs to know facts about itself: "What's my name? What namespace am I in? How much CPU was I promised?" But the app is sealed inside a container and can't see the Kubernetes paperwork. The **Downward API** is Kubernetes slipping that paperwork *down* into the container so the app can read it — hence "downward," info flowing down from the pod into the app.

You can deliver these facts two ways:

- **As environment variables** — handy for simple single values. Use `fieldRef` for pod facts (`metadata.name`, `metadata.namespace`) and `resourceFieldRef` for resource numbers (like the cpu limit). Here `POD_NAME`, `POD_NS`, and `CPU_LIMIT` all arrive as env vars.
- **As files in a folder** — via a `downwardAPI` volume. Here the pod's **labels** get written into a file at `/podinfo/labels`.

Why two ways? Because some facts simply **can't** be env vars. Labels and annotations can change while the pod runs, so Kubernetes will only expose them as **files** (which it keeps updated) — never as env vars (which are frozen at start).

**Watch out for:**

- **Labels and annotations can ONLY come through a volume**, never an env `fieldRef`. This is the headline gotcha.
- **Resource values use `resourceFieldRef`, not `fieldRef`**, and need a `containerName` to say whose limit you mean.
- **Pod identity fields (`metadata.name`, `metadata.namespace`) use `fieldRef`** and work fine as env vars.
- **Env vars are a snapshot at start;** volume-projected labels/annotations update live if they change.
- **The downwardAPI volume item needs a `path`** (the filename) and a `fieldRef`/`resourceFieldRef` — same shape as a projected-volume source.
questions.deepDive:
## Downward API — expose pod metadata

### Mental model
The **Downward API** injects a pod's own metadata and resource info into its containers — either as **environment variables** or as **files** in a `downwardAPI` volume. Two selector types: `fieldRef` (pod/object fields) and `resourceFieldRef` (container resource requests/limits).

### The manifest
```yaml
metadata:
  name: downward-pod
  namespace: pod-design
  labels: { app: downward }
spec:
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: busybox:1.36
    command: ["sh","-c","sleep 3600"]
    resources: { limits: { cpu: 500m } }
    env:
    - name: POD_NAME
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } }
    - name: POD_NS
      valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.namespace } }
    - name: CPU_LIMIT
      valueFrom: { resourceFieldRef: { containerName: app, resource: limits.cpu } }
    volumeMounts: [ { name: podinfo, mountPath: /podinfo } ]
  volumes:
  - name: podinfo
    downwardAPI:
      items: [ { path: labels, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.labels } } ]
```

### What you can expose — and how
| Field | env `fieldRef` | volume `fieldRef` |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata.name` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `metadata.namespace` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `metadata.uid` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `spec.nodeName`, `status.hostIP`, `status.podIP` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `spec.serviceAccountName` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `metadata.labels` | ❌ | ✅ **(volume only)** |
| `metadata.annotations` | ❌ | ✅ **(volume only)** |

### Resource fields (`resourceFieldRef`)
| Resource selector | Needs |
|---|---|
| `requests.cpu` / `limits.cpu` | `containerName`, `resource` |
| `requests.memory` / `limits.memory` | `containerName`, `resource` |
| `requests.ephemeral-storage` / `limits.*` | `containerName`, `resource` |

- Works both as env `valueFrom.resourceFieldRef` and in a `downwardAPI` volume item.
- Optional `divisor` normalises the value (e.g. `divisor: 1m` for CPU → millicores).

### env vs volume — key difference
| | env (`fieldRef`/`resourceFieldRef`) | downwardAPI volume |
|---|---|---|
| labels/annotations | ❌ not allowed | ✅ supported |
| updates after change | ❌ snapshot at start | ✅ labels/annotations refresh live |
| shape | one var per field | one file per `items[].path` |

### Verify
```bash
kubectl -n pod-design exec downward-pod -- env | grep -E 'POD_NAME|POD_NS|CPU_LIMIT'
kubectl -n pod-design exec downward-pod -- cat /podinfo/labels     # app="downward"
```

### Gotchas & exam traps
- **labels/annotations are volume-only** — attempting them as env `fieldRef` is rejected. Headline trap.
- **Resource values need `resourceFieldRef`** (not `fieldRef`) **and a `containerName`**.
- **`metadata.name`/`namespace`/`uid`, pod IP, node name** use `fieldRef` and work as env.
- **Env is a start-time snapshot**; volume-projected labels/annotations update live.
- **A `downwardAPI` volume item needs a `path`** plus a `fieldRef`/`resourceFieldRef` — same shape as a projected-volume `downwardAPI` source.
- `status.podIP` isn't known until scheduled — fine as env/volume, resolved at start.

### Quick reference
```yaml
env:
- { name: POD_NAME, valueFrom: { fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.name } } }
- { name: CPU_LIMIT, valueFrom: { resourceFieldRef: { containerName: app, resource: limits.cpu } } }
volumes:
- name: podinfo
  downwardAPI: { items: [ { path: labels, fieldRef: { fieldPath: metadata.labels } } ] }
```
